quote: In relative terms, StoneDB's bulk-insert throughput was about 54 percent higher than KVLite's.
problem: A2 gives 348 vs 212 thousand ops/s, which is about 64 percent higher (348/212 = 1.64), not 54.

quote: Marlin's higher write throughput comes from its batched write-ahead log, which groups concurrent writes into a single append.
problem: Causal mechanism stated as fact. The appendix only has a README line describing the write path; no profiler, tracing or ablation runs were collected (A1). It is an inference from documentation, not a measured cause.

quote: Marlin's write advantage holds regardless of storage hardware or durability settings.
problem: Overgeneralised. Everything was run on one machine with one NVMe SSD, and only batched fsync (every 1,000 writes) was used; per-write fsync was not tested (A1).

quote: Marlin also serves random reads faster than StoneDB.
problem: Not established. A2 gives Marlin 417 [391-426] and StoneDB 402 [395-410]: the medians differ by 15 and the min-max ranges overlap heavily (Marlin's minimum is below StoneDB's). The report itself treats a similarly small gap at 100M keys as unresolved.

quote: Under the mixed workload, KVLite's median p99 latency was 4.2 ms, the worst of the three, against 3.1 ms for StoneDB and 2.9 ms for Marlin.
problem: A3 gives KVLite's median p99 as 4.8 ms [4.5-5.2], not 4.2 ms.

quote: StoneDB sustains its mixed-workload throughput over long-running operation.
problem: Unsupported. The longest run was 6 minutes (5 measured) and no soak or multi-hour run was done (A1). A5 only covers five minutes and shows StoneDB rising from 262 to 270, so it says nothing about long-running behaviour.

quote: As for what the projects say about themselves, Marlin's own documentation presents it as the right engine for write-intensive systems generally.
problem: Misquotes the README (A7). It says Marlin is designed for write-intensive workloads whose reads mostly touch recently written keys, which is a narrower claim than 'generally'. The benchmark's reads were uniformly random.

quote: Wray kept a continuous day-by-day record of the winter.
problem: Contradicted by the appendix. Folios 31-34 are missing, and no entries are dated between 12 Dec 1741 and 26 Jan 1742 (46 days). The editor also says several entries were written up weeks later (E1, Q7).

quote: The vestry responded by laying a rate for the poor, recorded on folio 38v.
problem: The causal link to the mill closure is not in the source. The rate is on fol. 38v (Q3), before the mill passage on fol. 39v (Q4), and Wray does not link them. 'Responded' is the writer's inference, presented as what the journal says.

quote: The parish register shows 52 burials in 1742, which is 23 more than in 1741.
problem: E5(a) gives 52 in 1742 and 33 in 1741, a difference of 19, not 23.

quote: Of the 29 death entries in the journal, Wray names a fever as the cause in seven.
problem: E5(b) says fever is named in 5 of the 29 death entries, not 7.

quote: The frost alone accounts for the rise in burials in 1742.
problem: Unsupported causal claim. Cold or frost is named in only 6 of 29 death entries, fever is named in 5, and 18 name no cause (E5b). The register rise is 19 burials. 'Alone' is not shown, and the journal cannot establish it.

quote: Wray's burial entries have been checked against the parish register and found accurate.
problem: Overstated. Q8: the editor checked only nine of the burial notices (the journal has 29 death entries), found those nine matched, and says the remainder were not checked.

quote: Wray states that the vicar kept the tithe barn locked against the poor.
problem: Wray reports hearsay and disclaims it (Q5): 'It is said by some...I have not seen it with my own eyes', and the vicar says the barn is empty. Presenting it as Wray's own statement of fact misstates the source.

quote: The journal gives a representative picture of how rural parishes in the county fared that winter.
problem: Unsupported generalisation. The journal covers one parish and the edition prints no comparative material from any other parish (E1).

quote: Of the 48 nurses who were screened but not randomized, most (31) declined to take part.
problem: T2: 31 were ineligible and 17 declined. The figures for the two groups are swapped.

quote: Across both arms, 56 of 64 participants (85.9%) completed the week 8 assessment.
problem: 56/64 is 87.5%, as T2 shows. 85.9% is wrong.

quote: The reduction in insomnia severity persisted after the program ended.
problem: Assessments were at baseline and week 8 only, with no assessment after week 8 (T1) and no follow-up planned (T7 s6.3). The program was offered to the waitlist at week 8; persistence was never measured.

quote: The sleep-restriction module is what drove the improvement.
problem: Components were delivered together in a fixed sequence and the study does not test individual components (T7 s3.1). Attribution to one module is unsupported.

quote: Engagement with the program was high.
problem: T5 does not show it. Median 5 of 8 modules (IQR 3 to 8); only 11 of 32 (34.4%) completed all 8, and 8 of 32 completed 3 or fewer (2 completed none). No prespecified threshold for 'high' is given.

quote: These data show the program is safe for night-shift nurses.
problem: Overclaim. The protocol states the study is not powered to estimate adverse-event rate (T7 s7.4). N = 32 in the app arm, AEs were free-text self-report collected differently by arm (weekly check-in vs week 8 only), and the trial was open-label. Absence of serious events in a small pilot does not show safety.

quote: The findings apply to shift workers generally.
problem: Single-centre pilot of nurses at one teaching hospital with insomnia symptoms (T1). Efficacy is exploratory, so generalising to shift workers broadly is unsupported.

quote: Below 3.0 kN the bracket has an effectively infinite fatigue life.
problem: Nothing was tested below 3.0 kN (F3 note), and runout was capped at 2,000,000 cycles with no test continued beyond it (TP-221 4.3). This extrapolates well beyond the data from four specimens at the lowest level.

quote: One of the four specimens reached the runout and the other three failed, the shortest at 1,138,000 cycles.
problem: F3: the shortest 4.0 kN life is F4-04 at 1,238,000 cycles, not 1,138,000.

quote: At 4.0 kN the bracket has a 75 percent chance of failing before two million cycles.
problem: An in-sample 3-of-4 count presented as a probability. n = 4, one of those specimens was interrupted (F4-02), and no statistical analysis of the fatigue data was performed (F2).

quote: The mean life at 5.0 kN was about 483,000 cycles.
The excess set in S08 is explained by its coming from a different material lot.
problem: Unverified inference stated as explanation. S08 is a single specimen; the lot B mill certificate is not on file and no sectioning, hardness or tensile tests on lot B are scheduled (F5). Lot is confounded with anything else particular to S08.

quote: The bracket's performance carries over to the full range of service temperatures.
problem: REQ-EN-003 requires -30 C to +50 C, but all tests were at laboratory ambient, 20.1-22.6 C, with no tests at other temperatures (F2, F5).

quote: The fatigue programme was run in accordance with ASTM E466.
problem: TP-221 says the method was only 'adapted from' ASTM E466, with listed deviations: four specimens per level vs a plan target of six, and load frame alignment not verified (F1, F5).
